title: Former MLB Stars Find Cricket Skills Transfer Fast at Mumbai Kids Clinic
excerpt: Nick Swisher, Adrian Gonzalez and Jake Arrieta coached Hansraj Morarji School students in Mumbai, said the girls outperformed the boys, and pointed to Saturday's MLBx showdown with India's cricketers.
body:
• Former MLB stars Nick Swisher, Adrian Gonzalez and Jake Arrieta ran a baseball clinic for students at Hansraj Morarji School in Mumbai on October 23, with softball stars Rachel Garcia and Jordan Woolery leading sessions alongside them.
  • The coaches said cricket skills transferred directly: Gonzalez, a 317-home-run hitter, said India's bat-to-ball and catching skills are already advanced for a country with little baseball.
  • All the visiting players agreed the girls outperformed the boys, a point Garcia linked to the growth of women's sport in India.
  • The clinic leads into MLBx: Mumbai on Saturday, October 24 at Mumbai Football Arena, where the MLB legends join Indian cricketers Suryakumar Yadav, Deepak Chahar, Shardul Thakur and Radha Yadav for 3-on-3 baseball.

A schoolgirl with braided hair kept clearing the fence at a Mumbai playground on Thursday, and former New York Yankees first baseman Nick Swisher could not quite believe what he was watching. The students at Hansraj Morarji School had swapped their cricket gear for baseball gloves for a clinic run by a visiting group of Major League Baseball greats, according to Reuters.

"I am taking these kids back with me, they can really swing the bat," Swisher said after running home-run drills with the students.

Who Coached What

Swisher handled the home-run drills. Former Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Adrian Gonzalez and American softball star Rachel Garcia oversaw batting practice. Former Chicago Cubs pitcher Jake Arrieta, ex-Boston Red Sox outfielder and World Series champion Jonny Gomes and softball star Jordan Woolery ran the pitching and fielding sessions in Mumbai's heat.

Gonzalez, who hit 317 home runs across a 15-year MLB career, said the standard surprised him. "From how little baseball has been played in India, their skills are advanced," he said.

"I really feel like if India devoted time to baseball, you would have some Major League Baseball players in no time."

— Adrian Gonzalez, former Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman

Why Cricket Players Adapt So Fast

Gonzalez pointed to the overlap between the two bat-and-ball games: bat-to-ball skills and catching, especially catching with the hands rather than a glove-first technique. Swisher, who said he has been watching cricket himself, made the same point from the other side. "The cricket swing does transfer to the baseball swing," he said.

That transfer is the core of MLB's pitch in India. Ryo Takahashi, MLB's director of international business, said the league is not competing with cricket and put no timeline on expectations. "I think if kids play both, they'll be developing both skills in many ways," Takahashi said.

The Girls Stole the Show

The visiting players unanimously agreed that the girls consistently outperformed the boys at the clinic. Garcia connected that to a wider shift in Indian women's sport, which is also visible in the continued rise of Indian women's cricket. "I think the future for women in sports is growing. Hopefully in the next five to 10 years, we're going to be on top," Garcia said. "I'm excited to see what the future does look like and to keep inspiring young women to keep picking up a bat, ball or just going out there to try and play some sort of sport."

What Happens Next: MLBx Mumbai

The clinic was the grassroots warm-up for MLBx: Mumbai, the format's first edition in India, scheduled for Saturday, October 24 at Mumbai Football Arena in the Andheri Sports Complex. RevSportz reported that Radha Yadav and Venkatesh Iyer completed the lineup, joining India's T20 captain and MLB Ambassador Suryakumar Yadav, Shardul Thakur, Jitesh Sharma and Kashvee Gautam alongside the same MLB legends — Swisher, Gonzalez, Gomes and Arrieta — and AUSL stars Garcia and Woolery.

The 3-on-3 showdown represents four MLB franchises — the New York Yankees, Los Angeles Dodgers, Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs — and adds live performances by Badshah and KR$NA, interactive fan experiences and food. For Indian-American and NRI baseball fans, it is a rare case of the crossover running in the other direction: an American sport borrowing cricket's talent pool, on cricket's home turf, with India's own cricketers on the roster.
